title: Ajahn Funn: But in Pāli they don’t say, “die.” They say cuti—we move. When we leave here, why do we move? We can’t stay. Why…
content:
When We Discard the Body, Where Will We Go? Goodness Is Our Refuge

But in Pāli they don’t say, “die.” They say cuti—we move. When we leave here, why do we move? We can’t stay. Why can’t we stay? Because the four elements are no longer in harmony. We’re too hot, too cold, too heavy. These five aggregates are a heavy burden. They get so heavy that we’ve had enough—we can’t open our eyes, lift up our legs, get up and run. They get so heavy that we have to discard them.

So when we discard the body, where will we go? What will we be able to take with us? This is why the Buddha set out the religion, so that we can give rise to goodness and take that as our refuge. This is our practice. This is why he taught generosity, taught virtue, taught meditation. So acquaint yourselves with these things. They’re our provisions for the journey. When you develop goodness, no matter who you are, that goodness will protect you and take you to a good destination. So understand this. This is why I said that the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha are our refuge. Whatever we haven’t come to know, we won’t be able to do. Whatever we haven’t done, we won’t be able to depend on. Only the things that we’ve known and done and practiced will we be able to depend on.

title: Ajahn Funn: When we sit in meditation, our mind does not create becomings or births. The mind is still. It does not create any evil…
content:
When the Mind Has No Kamma, All Kamma Is Ended Right There

When we sit in meditation, our mind does not create becomings or births. The mind is still. It does not create any evil or kamma. It rests in equanimity. Then evil and kamma are ended right there. Not ended elsewhere. When our mind has no kamma, then all kamma is gone. When our mind has no evil, then all evil is gone. When our mind does not suffer, then all suffering is gone. When our mind does not crave, then all craving is gone.

Therefore, you should all contemplate this with certainty. Where else will you go to find happiness? Seeking happiness from rice, from possessions, from money and gold — that is not it. Seeking happiness from working and doing tasks — that is not it. We suffer precisely because we chase after possessions, money, and gold. This happiness must be achieved by making our mind still: Buddho, Buddho, making the mind cool and refreshed, making the mind light and at ease. When our heart is at ease, then our work is at ease, our possessions, money, and gold are at ease, the villagers and marketplaces are at ease, the whole country is at ease.

title: Ajahn Funn: What is in this body? Kesā — hair. How is hair clean? If it were clean, why do we wash and scrub it?…
content:
The 32 Parts: Hair, Body Hair, Nails, Teeth, Skin, Flesh, Tendons, Bones

What is in this body? Kesā — hair. How is hair clean? If it were clean, why do we wash and scrub it? Or if it were clean, could we pick fallen hair out of our rice and eat it? Could we? No, couldn't we? So how could it be clean? It is filled with impurities like this. We should contemplate to know it, to see it.

Lomā — body hair. Nakhā — nails. Dantā — teeth. Taco — skin. Maṃsaṃ — flesh. Filled like this. Nahāru — tendons. Aṭṭhi — bones. Aṭṭhimiñjaṃ — bone marrow. Vakkaṃ — kidneys. Hadayaṃ — heart. Yakanaṃ — liver. Kilomakaṃ — membranes. Pihakaṃ — spleen. Papphāsaṃ — lungs. Antaṃ — large intestine. Antaguṇaṃ — small intestine. Udariyaṃ — fresh food. Karīsaṃ — digested food. Filled with all these things — impurities. Look. We dwell in these things, and we call ourselves a person. Where is the person? They are just names, each one different. We must distinguish right here, then we will know Dhamma, see Dhamma. If we do not distinguish like this, we give rise to diṭṭhi (wrong view), māna (conceit), ahaṃkāra (egoism), mamaṃkāra (possessiveness), holding that we are a person, a self, a being, an individual, a "me" or "him," a woman or a man, a monk or a novice.

title: Ajahn Funn: We all dwell with the Divine Messengers (devadūta) every day, every moment, every minute. What are the devadūta? They are birth, aging, sickness,…
content:
The Divine Messengers: Birth, Aging, Sickness, and Death

We all dwell with the Divine Messengers (devadūta) every day, every moment, every minute. What are the devadūta? They are birth, aging, sickness, and death. These are what we see. We all wish to be free from suffering. Suffering is nothing else. The Buddha taught us to see these devadūta.

When a person sees the devadūta and knows the devadūta, that person will be freed from suffering. Suffering is not something else. Suffering is not about having no place to live, not about lacking material goods or money, not about having no rank or status. That is not it. The Buddha did not call those things suffering. Suffering is already inherent in everyone: we cannot escape birth, cannot escape aging, cannot escape sickness, cannot escape death. It is already there. The way to escape it, the Buddha taught a refuge: take the Buddha as refuge, take the Dhamma and the Noble Saṅgha as refuge, as a place of refuge to pay homage and worship every day. When we reach the Buddha, we will be freed. If we do not take the Buddha as refuge, we cannot be freed.

title: Ajahn Funn: This is why, after the Buddha gained awakening, he set out the religion as a series of daily practices: virtue, concentration, discernment. These…
content:
The Three Levels of Virtue: Five, Eight/Ten, and 227 Precepts

This is why, after the Buddha gained awakening, he set out the religion as a series of daily practices: virtue, concentration, discernment. These are the basic principles of the religion. On the lowest level, there’s generosity, virtue, and meditation. The Buddha taught these as daily practices: the lower level of virtue, the medium level of virtue, the refined level of virtue. The lower level is the five precepts. The medium level is the eight or ten precepts. The refined level is the 227 training rules for the monks.

In the 227 training rules, the Buddha taught everything: how to wear your robes, how to eat, how to sit, how to lie down, how to walk, how to stand. He taught everything—even how to chew a mouthful of rice, how to put the rice in your mouth: He even taught that. How so? Make the mouthful rounded, not too big, and don’t bite a piece from a handful of rice. Don’t throw it into your mouth. As long as the rice hasn’t come to your mouth, don’t open your mouth. Don’t make chomping noises like pigs. Don’t make slurping noises. Don’t nibble from your handful. Don’t lick your lips. Don’t lick your hands. He taught down to the details like this—so that your behavior will be gracious.

title: Ajahn Funn: This is how the Buddha taught in the past. Those who heard and received his instructions attained the path and fruit – many…
content:
The Two Extremes: Attraction and Aversion – Walk the Middle Way

This is how the Buddha taught in the past. Those who heard and received his instructions attained the path and fruit – many becoming stream-enterers (sotāpanna), once-returners (sakadāgāmī), non-returners (anāgāmī), and arahants (arahatta). But nowadays, even though we listen, no one is seen to attain the religion. Why? Because we only listen to the sound. We say a good sound is good – but what is actually good? We must make it opanayiko – bring it down into our hearts. You want to be good: is your heart good yet? If the heart is not good, you will not be good.

In the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta he said: "Bhikkhus, do not indulge in these two extremes. Walk the middle way." What are the two extremes? They are attraction on one side and aversion on the other. If we cling to either one, we suffer.

Therefore, he does not let us cling to them. He tells us to walk the middle way. It's like walking through a rough path: if you turn to this side, you get thorns; if you turn to that side, you get thorns. If you don't turn off, but walk straight ahead, there is no suffering, isn't that so?

title: Ajahn Funn: Āyaṃ attabhāvo – this existence, this birth, is dukkhaṃ, aniccaṃ, anattā – impermanent, suffering, not self, not a being. Asuci, asubhaṃ – it…
content:
Contemplate the Funeral: All Beings Die – There Is No Doubt

Āyaṃ attabhāvo – this existence, this birth, is dukkhaṃ, aniccaṃ, anattā – impermanent, suffering, not self, not a being. Asuci, asubhaṃ – it is just a pool of pus and filth, all the same. Imaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ bhaveti – one should develop meditation to see it that way.

The teachers tell us to contemplate ourselves to see it that way. Aniccā vata saṅkhārā – indeed, formations are like this. They are all impermanent. We should not be deluded. Contemplate to know and see. We don't get entangled in anything, don't cling to anything. No entanglement with children, grandchildren, home, city. This one has no entanglement. No clinging to status. No clinging to anything at all. Nothing entangles. Do you see? We should focus to know and see. Why is a person happy? It is because of the calming of saṅkhārā – vūpasamo sukho – happiness due to the stilling of formations. Sabbe sattā maranti ca, mariṃsu ca marissare; tathevāhaṃ marissāmi, natthi me ettha saṃsayo – "All beings die, have died, and will die; just so, I too will die; there is no doubt about this." Don't doubt. We all must be like this. Beings have died. Those alive now will also die. We need not doubt. What else is there to doubt? What can we gain from anything at all?

title: Ajahn Funn: Therefore, the teaching is to let go, to give up everything. How can you let go? When it sees suffering, it lets go…
content:
There Is No Happiness Equal to the Peace of Mind

Therefore, the teaching is to let go, to give up everything. How can you let go? When it sees suffering, it lets go by itself. If it doesn’t see, it won’t let go. When it sees, it lets go. It releases, gives up, abandons, withdraws by itself. The mind can remain still. There is only lightness, ease, brightness, clarity, coolness, and calm. The crucial point is that it is happy and at ease. What can compare? Natthi santi paraṃ sukhaṃ — there is no happiness equal to the peace of mind. It receives happiness and ease, fulfilling our aspirations.

When we see this, we are free from suffering. If our mind is not suffering, what could make it suffer? It becomes free right there. That mind-element is free from suffering. Where could it find suffering? It has buddho, dhammo, saṅgho; it has adorned itself with the Three Jewels. Then we have clear knowing and true seeing. We no longer believe anyone else. We see for ourselves, certainly: sanditthiko. As practitioners, we know and see for ourselves. How could we not see? When at ease, how could we not see? When not at ease, how could we not see? When it sees, it remains confident like that. These things really exist — it’s not that they don’t exist. They truly exist. They exist in our mind. When it’s still, it sees. When it’s not still, it sees. However it is, it sees.

title: Ajahn Funn: The Buddha taught us to cultivate sīla, samādhi, paññā as the foundation of the Buddhist teachings. Cultivating sīla means restraining body, speech, and…
content:
Cultivating Sīla: Restraining Body, Speech, and Mind

The Buddha taught us to cultivate sīla, samādhi, paññā as the foundation of the Buddhist teachings. Cultivating sīla means restraining body, speech, and mind to be calm and proper. We restrain the body, compose our body, speech, and mind to be proper. If we do no wrong, great or small, by body, speech, or mind, then when we are reborn we will not be deformed or disabled. We will be born with complete body, complete speech, complete mind. This is what we want. Keeping sīla is nothing else; it is keeping body, speech, and mind. Just this. Keeping it so that we ourselves may escape from falling into misery and difficulty, so that our body is not deformed or disabled, our mind is not deranged. Keep right here.

This is the path to escape from suffering. Let us all do this. Sammā-samādhi – make the mind steady. Do not let it go and produce bhava and jāti, produce kamma and enmity. The mind is peaceful because of samādhi; the mind is established, steady, upright. The mind does not waver or vacillate in forms, sounds, smells, tastes, or tactile objects. When it goes out, it goes out to produce great and small bhava and jāti. Therefore, we should go to the monastery and look.

title: Ajahn Funn: Moreover, we come to make merit and wholesome qualities, to do good deeds, so that we receive happiness and ease. When our mind…
content:
When Everyone Has Virtue and Dhamma, Evil Dissolves by Itself Like Darkness Before Fire

Moreover, we come to make merit and wholesome qualities, to do good deeds, so that we receive happiness and ease. When our mind receives happiness and ease, then there are no issues, no problems. Our country becomes peaceful and calm. This is why you must learn to reach the heart and understand. If we are good, even if others are not good – all people, every single one, even the tiny red ant or the little insect – all want goodness. Those who behave badly, who do evil, cannot survive. It is because of this goodness that things are that way. Now, anyone who tries to destroy a good person will themselves be ruined – the destroyer himself. When in our country everyone has virtue and Dhamma, everyone has merit and wholesomeness, everyone is happy, the mind happy and at ease, then evil will dissolve by itself. It is like lighting a fire: the darkness disappears on its own. Those wrong-doers who bring other countries to destroy us – the earth will swallow them up. Just watch. We have taken the Buddha as our refuge. If we go taking other things as refuge and recollection, and just keep trying to revolt and force each other, will it work? Anyone who persecutes the Buddha – the earth really swallows them. So it is.
